periods.activity_title: Weaving Rules: Making and Decoding Paper Mats

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
tasks_in_class.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.
Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.
Work out the steps for either of the two shown weave designs; write the pattern for each row until it starts repeating.

homework.description: Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

time_bands.activity: Each student folds a sheet of coloured paper, cuts slits, and weaves 8 colour strips using the alternating over-under rule: Let us make paper mats, p.92 ("Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips...."). As strips go in, the teacher names the rule aloud — one under, one over — and students check each other's weave.

Students look at a drawn 2-over-1-under mat: Q2, p.93 ("Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven...."). Pairs study the first two rows and write the row rule in words. The class pools rules and the teacher captures two or three versions on the board, asking 'Which is the shortest way to say this?'

Students choose one design from Q4, p.93 ("Work out the steps for either of the two shown weave designs....") and write the row-by-row rule until it begins to repeat. Groups compare: do different students who chose the same design write the same rule? Teacher notes that a repeating unit is the fingerprint of any weave pattern, and introduces Let Us Try, p.93 ("Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper....") as an unhurried grid task to complete at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The key idea is that a weave is generated by one repeating rule, not memorised row by row — so press students to state the shortest rule that reconstructs every row. A common error is reversing the rule for odd and even rows; ask a student to predict row 3 from their rule and check it against the mat. Q3, p.93 is an additional making task for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Fitting Shapes at a Point: Who Tessellates?

tasks_in_class.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.
Try fitting square cutouts around a point without any gap or overlap; count how many squares are needed.
Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.
Try drawing regular octagons together to check whether they tessellate without gaps or overlaps.

time_bands.activity: Each group receives a set of pre-cut regular triangles and fits them around a single point on paper: Find Out, p.94 ("Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap...."). They count how many fit and record. Teacher introduces the word 'tessellate' — shapes that cover a surface with no gaps or overlaps.

Groups switch to square cutouts: Find Out, p.94 ("Try fitting square cutouts around a point without any gap or overlap...."). They count and record. Then: Find Out, p.94 ("Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps?"). Students try physically and explain in a sentence why five do not fit — too many or not enough? Teacher collects one or two explanations and introduces the idea of equal sides defining a 'regular' shape.

Groups test hexagon cutouts at a point: Find Out, p.94 ("Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point...."). Count and record. Finally, students attempt to draw regular octagons side by side: Find Out, p.95 ("Try drawing regular octagons together to check whether they tessellate...."). They observe and record the result — gap or no gap?

Class builds a shared table on the board: shape name, how many fit at a point, tessellates yes/no. Teacher asks: 'What do the yes-shapes have in common?' Students articulate that triangles, squares, and hexagons tessellate; pentagons and octagons do not. The teacher notes that the physical test at a point is the check, not guessing from the picture.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical reasoning step is T-8 — students often think 'almost fitting' is fine; hold them to the physical test: does every copy seat flush with no sliver of gap? A common error is using non-regular triangles from scrap paper; ensure cutouts are truly equilateral, square, and regular hexagonal. T-10 (multi-shape patterns on grid) is held back for the pattern-extension work, so this unit closes on the single-shape investigation.

periods.activity_title: Multi-Shape Tilings: Extending and Colouring Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern on the grid and colour it appropriately.
Identify shapes meeting at marked points in the octagon+square tiling; check if same shapes meet at all points; continue and colour the pattern.
In the square+triangle tiling: identify shapes at marked points; check consistency; continue and colour it; reason whether triangles are equilateral.
Create similar tiling patterns using other cutouts of shapes.

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.95 and name the two shapes in the partial pattern: Find Out, p.95 ("Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern...."). They continue the pattern on dot/grid paper in pencil, then colour the two shapes in contrasting colours. Teacher circulates, checking that extensions preserve the arrangement.

Students move to the octagon+square tiling: Find Out, p.96 ("Identify shapes meeting at marked points in the octagon+square tiling...."). They name shapes at each marked point, check whether the same combination appears at every point, continue the tiling, and colour it. The teacher draws attention to the idea that a consistent arrangement at every vertex is what makes a tiling 'regular'.

Students tackle the square+triangle tiling: Find Out, p.96 ("In the square+triangle tiling: identify shapes at marked points...."). After naming shapes, they reason about whether the triangles are equilateral by comparing their sides to the square's sides. Brief pair-discussion: 'How do you know?'

Open exploration: Find Out, p.96 ("Create similar tiling patterns using other cutouts of shapes...."). Students choose any combination of cutouts and test whether a tiling results, tracing the result on paper. A few students share their attempts; the class judges — gap, overlap, or a true tiling?

periods.teacher_notes: Students working on multi-shape tilings often colour inconsistently, making it hard to see the repeating arrangement; insist on a fixed colour per shape type throughout. A frequent misconception in T-13 is that 'the triangles look equilateral' without evidence — push students to compare a triangle side to the square side to settle it. T-14 is deliberately open; accept any genuine attempt even if a tiling does not succeed, as the negative result also builds understanding.
materials: Pre-cut shape cutouts (octagons, squares, triangles, hexagons)

periods.activity_title: Cutting and Classifying: Triangles from Rhombus Pieces

tasks_in_class.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.
How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle) from the rhombus pieces?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal (scalene) from the rhombus pieces?
Cut equilateral triangle; fold to check all angles are equal; cut in half; observe the resulting scalene triangle and check its angles.

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts a rhombus into four congruent triangles. They fit two pieces together in different orientations, trace each shape formed, and name the shape: Try This, p.97 ("Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify...."). The teacher models the first arrangement and names the activity 'discovering shapes inside shapes'.

Students count distinct triangle types they can make with two pieces — Try This Q1, p.97 ("How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces?"). They measure sides with a ruler and record equal/unequal relationships. Teacher introduces isosceles (two equal sides) and reinforces the vocabulary from measurement, not from memory.

Focused reasoning: Try This Q2, p.97 ("Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal....?") and Try This Q3, p.97 ("Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal....?"). Students try and record yes/no with a sketch. Class discussion: what do the rhombus piece's side lengths allow and forbid?

Students cut a separate equilateral triangle, fold it to confirm equal angles, then cut it in half and examine the two scalene pieces: Try This, p.97 ("Cut equilateral triangle; fold to check all angles are equal; cut in half...."). They compare sides and angles of the scalene piece to those of their rhombus triangles and record one observation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse isosceles (two equal sides) with equilateral (three equal sides) at this stage — ask them to use a ruler to confirm before naming. A common error in T-17 and T-18 is claiming a result without trying all arrangements; insist on physical testing with the pieces before writing an answer. The classification — equilateral, isosceles, scalene — arises from the measurement, so keep rulers in hand throughout.
materials: Rhombus-shaped coloured card (one per student, pre-drawn for cutting)
Separate equilateral triangle card for T-19

periods.activity_title: From Three and Four Pieces: Quadrilaterals and Polygons

tasks_in_class.description: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make by fitting 2 rhombus triangles? Explore the possibilities.
Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B; find equal pairs (adjacent or opposite); identify what types of angles each has.
Use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes; count sides of each; try creating a 3-sided, 4-sided, and 5-sided shape.
Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can be made.

homework.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.

time_bands.activity: Students use their four rhombus-triangle pieces (cut in the previous exploration or a fresh pre-cut set) and fit two together to form as many distinct quadrilaterals as possible: Try This Q4, p.98 ("How many different 4-sided shapes can you make by fitting 2 rhombus triangles?"). They trace each shape and count — the goal is systematic listing, not guessing.

Students measure the sides of quadrilaterals A and B from the textbook: Try This Q5, p.98 ("Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B; find equal pairs...."). They label equal sides and record whether equal pairs are adjacent or opposite, and name the angle types present. Teacher introduces 'adjacent' and 'opposite' sides using the shapes in hand.

Using three pieces, students try to form a 3-sided, a 4-sided, and a 5-sided shape: Try This Q7, p.99 ("Use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes; count sides of each...."). They trace successes and record which side-counts are achievable. Unsuccessful attempts are also noted.

All four pieces now: Try This Q8, p.99 ("Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes — square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon — can be made...."). Students check each named shape systematically. Teacher assigns Try This Q6, p.99 ("Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given....") as an unhurried drawing task for home.

periods.teacher_notes: In T-21, students often see 'equal sides' but do not distinguish adjacent from opposite — use a finger trace around the shape to show which sides share a corner (adjacent) and which face each other (opposite). Students working on T-24 should tick or cross each shape name as they test it rather than relying on memory; systematic checking prevents missed cases. The classification of kite vs. parallelogram that emerges from T-21 prepares the vocabulary needed.

periods.activity_title: Which Shape Am I? Kites, Tangrams, and Quadrilateral Properties

tasks_in_class.description: Cut out tangram shapes; compare sides and angles of each piece; use some or all pieces to make the given shapes (parallelogram, rectangle, triangle, trapezoid).
Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.
Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

time_bands.activity: Students cut out tangram pieces from the textbook or a printed sheet and compare sides and angles of each piece by placing them together: Tangram, p.99 ("Cut out tangram shapes; compare sides and angles of each piece...."). They then arrange pieces to make the parallelogram, rectangle, triangle, and trapezoid shown, tracing each result.

Students read each of the 7 property statements in Which Shape Am I?, p.100 ("Match 7 property statements to the correct shape....") and write the shape or shapes each statement fits — square, rectangle, rhombus, or parallelogram. Pairs compare answers and discuss statements that match more than one shape, with the teacher noting that a square is a special rectangle and a special rhombus.

Each student takes a square sheet of paper and makes a kite by folding the diagonal, then folding corners A and B inward: Kites, p.100 ("Make a kite by paper-folding from a square; fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward...."). They open the kite slightly and name the shapes visible inside (triangles). Teacher draws out: two pairs of adjacent equal sides — different from the opposite-equal-sides of a parallelogram.

periods.teacher_notes: The central conceptual step is that kite-ness is about ADJACENT equal sides while parallelogram-ness is about OPPOSITE equal sides — confusion between these two is the most common error at this stage. In the 'Which Shape Am I?' task, students often assign each statement to only one shape and miss that a square satisfies parallelogram statements too; press them to test every shape against every statement. The paper-folding kite is a reinforcement through making, not a separate concept.

section_titles: Play with Circles and Circle Designs

tasks_in_class.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.
Join numbered circle points (1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, ...) to make a string-art design; think of a way to make the overlapping-circles image.

time_bands.activity: Students draw a circle with a compass, mark two diameters (any orientation), and join the four endpoints to form a quadrilateral: Play with Circles, p.101 ("Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed...."). They measure the four angles with a protractor or fold to compare. Each student tries a second pair of diameters at a different angle and records what shape they get. Class discussion: does the shape change when the diameters are at a different angle?

Students receive or draw a circle with 12 equally spaced numbered points. Following the skip rule (1→11, 11→2, 2→12, ...), they draw chords one by one: Circle Designs, p.101 ("Join numbered circle points to make a string-art design...."). As the design grows they observe the emerging curved pattern. Students then think about and sketch a plan for how the overlapping-circles image on the same page might be made.

periods.teacher_notes: In T-28, students often draw two diameters that happen to be perpendicular and conclude that joining diameter-endpoints always gives a square — insist they try a non-perpendicular pair and measure to find it is still a rectangle but not a square. For T-29, the visual effect only appears once enough chords are drawn; encourage students not to stop after three or four lines. The idea that a sequence of straight lines can create the appearance of a curve is the key observation to draw out in discussion.
materials: Circle template with 12 numbered points (printed or drawn)

periods.activity_title: Nets, Removed Cubes, Painted Faces, and a Shape Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.
Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).
Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.
Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

time_bands.activity: Students study the three views of a cube shown in the textbook and map each face pattern to its position on the net: Cube Connections Q1, p.102 ("Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net...."). The teacher models mentally 'folding' one face to find where it lands, then students complete independently.

Students examine each cube-frame picture and count how many small cubes are missing: Cube Connections Q2, p.102 ("Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each...."). They use the total-cube count minus the remaining-cube count, or count removed spaces directly. Pairs compare strategies.

Students work through the painted-cube puzzle: Cube Connections Q3, p.102 ("Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces...."). Teacher prompts: 'Which positions touch exactly three faces of the big cube?' Students work systematically through corner, edge, face-centre, and interior positions and write the four counts.

Students read the five clues in Puzzle, p.102 ("Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes in a line....") and use elimination to place shapes one by one. Those who finish record their arrangement; early completers try to find whether any other arrangement also satisfies all five clues.

periods.teacher_notes: The painted-cube problem (T-32) is the most demanding task in this unit; the most common error is double-counting edge cubes as corner cubes — prompt students to ask 'how many faces of the BIG cube does this small cube touch?' before assigning a category. For T-31, students sometimes subtract from the wrong total; establish 'how many small cubes in a solid 3×3×3?' before any subtraction. T-33 is best done on a rough strip of paper where students write shape names in seven slots and cross out and rewrite as each clue eliminates options.
materials: Rough paper strips for the puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

time_bands.activity: Students carefully cut out the net for the icosahedron from the back of the book (or a printed copy), score fold lines, and glue tabs to assemble the solid: Icosahedron and Dodecahedron, p.103 ("Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models...."). Teacher circulates, helping students keep fold directions consistent so the model closes correctly.

Students repeat the process for the dodecahedron net. Once both models are assembled, they record observations: what shape is each face? Are all faces the same shape? How many faces meet at each vertex? Students count edges by running a finger along each edge and tallying.

Class shares findings. The teacher builds a comparison table on the board: solid name, face shape, number of faces, faces at each vertex, edge count. Students check their own models against the class table and correct any counting errors. Open question to close the unit: 'How do these two solids compare with the cube we investigated?' Students name at least one similarity and one difference.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in model-building is folding tabs the wrong way, which prevents the net from closing — show students to fold all tabs away from the printed face before gluing. When counting edges, students tend to recount the same edge from two faces; suggest they mark each edge with a pencil dot as they count it. The comparison with the cube (six square faces, three faces at each vertex) anchors the new vocabulary — faces, vertices, edges — in a shape students already know.
materials: Icosahedron net (from back of textbook or printed copy, one per student)
Pencils for marking edges during counting

items.prompt: Look at this weave rule: Row 1 — go OVER 1 strip, then UNDER 1 strip, and repeat. Row 2 — go UNDER 1 strip, then OVER 1 strip, and repeat. Draw or write what Row 3 and Row 4 would look like if this rule continues.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3 is the same as Row 1: over 1, under 1, repeating. Row 4 is the same as Row 2: under 1, over 1, repeating. The pattern repeats every 2 rows.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the repeating unit (2 rows) and continue it forward.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student colour strips on a drawn grid to see the pattern; stretch: ask them to write the rule for a 2-over-1-under mat.

exercise.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
exercise.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.

items.prompt: Riya places regular triangle cutouts around a single point, fitting them edge-to-edge with no gaps. How many triangles fit exactly around the point?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 equilateral triangles fit exactly around a point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Physically fit triangles around a point and count until the ring closes without gap or overlap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing triangles with squares, where 4 fit at a point.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have stopped counting before the ring closed, leaving a small gap.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be double-counting or confusing with the number of sides in an octagon.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use physical triangle cutouts to fit around a drawn point; stretch: ask how many squares would fit at a point and why the answer is different.

exercise.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.

items.prompt: Priya places regular hexagon cutouts around a single point, fitting them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps. How many hexagons fit exactly around the point?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 regular hexagons fit exactly around a point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit hexagon cutouts around a point and count until the ring closes without gap or overlap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think only two hexagons can share a corner, confusing edges with vertices.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be confusing hexagons with squares, where 4 fit at a point.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confusing the number of sides of a hexagon with how many fit at a vertex.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace three hexagons around a drawn point to confirm; stretch: ask whether the same result holds for a non-regular hexagon and why.

exercise.description: Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.

items.prompt: Anu tries to tile a surface using only regular octagons. She notices a problem. What is the problem, and what does she need to add to fill the gaps?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Regular octagons leave square-shaped gaps when placed together, so they do not tessellate on their own. Anu needs to add small squares to fill the gaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw octagons side by side and observe the shape of the space left between them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two octagons side by side on grid paper and trace the gap shape; stretch: ask the student to name the resulting two-shape tiling and describe what meets at each vertex.

exercise.description: Try drawing regular octagons together to check whether they tessellate without gaps or overlaps.

items.prompt: Deepa makes a tiling pattern using two different shapes. She notices that the same combination of shapes meets at every vertex. Name one pair of shapes that can tile together this way, and write the shapes that meet at each shared vertex.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid answer: octagons and squares — at each vertex, 2 octagons and 1 square meet. Another valid answer: squares and equilateral triangles — at each vertex, 2 squares and 3 triangles (or other consistent combinations) meet.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Continue the two-shape tiling on dot paper and check the shapes listed at one marked vertex against every other vertex.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use cutouts and trace around a single vertex; stretch: ask the student to continue the pattern for at least four more tiles and check consistency at two additional vertices.

exercise.description: Create similar tiling patterns using other cutouts of shapes.

items.prompt: Meera cuts a rhombus into four equal triangles. She fits two triangles together along their longest sides. Draw or name two different shapes she could make. What do these two shapes have in common?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She can make a larger isosceles triangle (two short sides meeting) or a parallelogram (long sides meeting). Both shapes have sides whose lengths come from the rhombus triangle's sides, so at least two sides in each shape are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit two rhombus triangles in different orientations, trace each result, and name the shape by counting sides.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn rhombus for the student to cut and physically try two arrangements; stretch: ask how many totally different shapes can be made from two pieces and to list all of them.

exercise.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.

items.prompt: Raj has four triangles cut from a rhombus. He wants to make a rectangle using all four pieces. Can he do it? Write yes or no, and draw the arrangement or explain why not.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Arrange the four triangles so that two form a parallelogram and the other two mirror them, or pair them into two identical parallelograms placed side by side to form a rectangle. The answer is yes — a rectangle (which is also a parallelogram) can be made.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pair four rhombus triangles into two parallelograms and place them flush to form a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use physical pieces and try several arrangements on paper; stretch: ask which other shapes from the named list (square, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can also be made from all four pieces.

exercise.description: Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can be made.

items.prompt: Sana folds a square piece of paper along its diagonal, then folds corner A inward, then corner B inward, to make a kite. She opens the kite and looks inside. Name two shapes she can see inside the folded kite.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She can see triangles inside the kite — the fold lines create triangular regions. She may also observe smaller kite-like shapes depending on how far the corners are folded.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the square into a kite and trace the fold lines to identify the triangular regions created.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and unfold to see the crease lines clearly; stretch: ask how many triangles are visible and whether any two triangles are the same size.

exercise.description: Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

items.section_title: Play with Circles and Circle Designs
items.prompt: Tara draws a circle, marks two diameters, and joins the four endpoints to form a shape. What shape does she always get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She always gets a rectangle. The four endpoints lie on the circle, and joining them in order forms a rectangle because both diameters are equal in length and bisect each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Join the four diameter-endpoints in order and measure or fold to confirm all angles are right angles.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have tried only perpendicular diameters, which do give a square — a special case not the general rule.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of the rhombus formed by the four radius segments rather than the joined endpoints.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confusing the shape with a figure formed by non-diametric chords.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two diameter pairs — one perpendicular, one not — and compare the shapes; stretch: ask what special kind of rectangle forms when the two diameters are perpendicular.

exercise.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.

items.prompt: Arjun builds an icosahedron from its net. He wants to record its properties. Write: (a) the shape of each face, (b) how many faces meet at each vertex, and (c) whether all faces are the same shape.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Each face is an equilateral triangle. (b) Five triangular faces meet at each vertex. (c) Yes, all faces are the same shape — equilateral triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build the model from the net, then count faces at one vertex and check a second vertex to confirm the same number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold the completed model and point to one vertex while counting faces aloud with a partner; stretch: ask the student to compare the number of faces at a vertex in the icosahedron with the number in the dodecahedron.

exercise.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

items.prompt: A mat is woven with this rule: Row 1 — OVER 2, UNDER 1, repeat. Row 2 — UNDER 1, OVER 2, repeat. A student says Row 5 will look the same as Row 2. Is the student correct? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. The rule repeats every 2 rows, so odd rows (1, 3, 5, …) are all the same as Row 1, and even rows (2, 4, 6, …) are the same as Row 2. Row 5 is odd, so it looks like Row 1, not Row 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the 2-row repeating unit and use odd/even position to determine which row pattern applies.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out rows 1–6 in a list and ask the student to colour-code odd and even rows; stretch: ask what the rule would be if the pattern repeated every 3 rows instead of 2.

exercise.description: Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.

items.prompt: A student writes this rule for a weave design: Row 1 — over 3, under 1, over 3, under 1, … ; Row 2 — under 2, over 1, under 2, over 1, … ; Row 3 — same as Row 1. At what row does the pattern first repeat from the beginning?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pattern first repeats at Row 3, which is the same as Row 1. The repeating unit is 2 rows long (Row 1 and Row 2).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write out rows until one matches Row 1 exactly; that row number is where repetition first occurs.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write rows 1, 2, 3 side by side and ask the student to compare Row 3 to Row 1 strip by strip; stretch: ask the student to design their own 3-row repeating weave rule.

exercise.description: Work out the steps for either of the two shown weave designs; write the pattern for each row until it starts repeating.

items.prompt: Veer places square tiles around a single point. He fills the space exactly with no gap. He then tries to place a 5th square. What happens, and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The 5th square does not fit — 4 squares already fill the space around the point completely, so adding a 5th would cause an overlap. Exactly 4 squares fill 360° around a point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: 4 squares fill 360° around a point (each square corner is 90°, and 4 × 90° = 360°), so a 5th would overlap.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use square cutouts to physically check; stretch: ask what angle each corner of a regular hexagon has and how many hexagons would fit at a point.

exercise.description: Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?

items.prompt: In the octagon-and-square tiling, Leena marks a point where three shapes meet. She writes: '2 octagons and 1 square meet here.' She then checks three more marked points. What should she find at each one, and why is this important for the tiling?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She should find exactly 2 octagons and 1 square at every marked point. This consistency — the same combination of shapes at every vertex — is what makes the tiling regular and allows it to cover the surface without gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Continue the tiling on dot paper and list the shapes meeting at each of several marked vertices to confirm the same combination repeats.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed partial tiling and ask them to circle and label just two vertices; stretch: ask how this differs from a tiling where the combination at vertices varies.

exercise.description: Identify shapes meeting at marked points in the octagon+square tiling; check if same shapes meet at all points; continue and colour the pattern.

items.prompt: Kiran fits two rhombus triangles together and makes a triangle. She measures the sides and finds two sides are each 4 cm and one side is 5 cm. What type of triangle is this? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: It is an isosceles triangle, because exactly two sides are equal (both 4 cm) and the third side is different (5 cm).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the three measured side lengths: two equal sides and one different side identifies an isosceles triangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the three side lengths in a list and ask the student to circle any that are equal; stretch: ask what measurement change would make it equilateral and whether that is possible with rhombus pieces.

exercise.description: How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?

items.prompt: Priya measures two quadrilaterals made from rhombus triangles. Shape A has two pairs of opposite equal sides. Shape B has two pairs of adjacent equal sides. What type of quadrilateral is each?

options.label: C
options.text: Shape A is a kite; Shape B is a parallelogram.

options.label: D
options.text: Shape A is a parallelogram; Shape B is a kite.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape A is a parallelogram (opposite sides equal); Shape B is a kite (adjacent sides equal in two pairs).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the defining properties: parallelogram — opposite sides equal; kite — two pairs of adjacent sides equal.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has swapped the definitions of kite and parallelogram.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies only the parallelogram property and does not recognise the kite's adjacent-equal-sides feature.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student applies only the kite property and does not recognise the parallelogram's opposite-equal-sides feature.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple labelled diagram of each shape with side-equality marks before asking the student to name it; stretch: ask whether a rhombus satisfies both kite and parallelogram properties and why.

exercise.description: Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B; find equal pairs (adjacent or opposite); identify what types of angles each has.

items.prompt: Read this property: 'All four sides are equal and all four angles are right angles.' Which shape or shapes does this describe?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only a square has all four sides equal AND all four angles as right angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each shape against both conditions: equal sides AND right angles — only the square satisfies both simultaneously.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises the right-angle condition but forgets that a rectangle's sides are not all equal.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognises the equal-sides condition but forgets that a rhombus does not require right angles.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly includes the square but also adds the rectangle, forgetting that a rectangle does not require all sides to be equal.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the four shapes with side-equality marks and angle marks, then ask the student to tick which marks each shape has; stretch: ask whether a square is also a special rectangle and a special rhombus, and justify both answers.

exercise.description: Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.

items.prompt: A cube has a star on the top face, a circle on the front face, and a triangle on the right face. Arun is given the net of this cube. He needs to place the star, circle, and triangle on the correct faces of the net. Describe how he decides which net-face gets each symbol.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arun mentally folds the net to match each face's position: the face that folds to the top gets the star, the face that folds to the front gets the circle, and the face that folds to the right gets the triangle. He checks by imagining which faces become adjacent after folding.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mentally fold the net step by step, tracking which flat face becomes which 3D face of the cube.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cut and fold the net physically to check the placement; stretch: ask the student to determine what symbol is on the bottom face and the back face, using the three given views.

exercise.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.

items.prompt:
Seven shapes — 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle — are placed in a row. Here are the clues:
1. The circle is in the middle.
2. A square is next to the circle on the left.
3. A triangle is at the right end.
4. The hexagon is between the two triangles.
5. The rectangle is at the left end.
In what order are the shapes placed from left to right?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Left to right: rectangle, square, circle, hexagon, triangle, square, triangle. Wait — let us re-derive carefully. 7 positions. Clue 1: circle is position 4 (middle of 7). Clue 2: square is position 3. Clue 3: triangle is at position 7. Clue 4: hexagon is between the two triangles — so the two triangles are on either side of the hexagon; with one triangle at position 7, the hexagon is at position 6 and the second triangle is at position 5. Clue 5: rectangle is at position 1. Remaining shape: square — must go to position 2. Final order: rectangle, square, square, circle, triangle, hexagon, triangle. Check clue 2: a square is next to the circle on the left — position 3 is a square next to circle at position 4. Confirmed. Final answer: Rectangle, Square, Square, Circle, Triangle, Hexagon, Triangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the circle at position 4, use each clue to fix one more shape, and fill the remaining position with the leftover shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student seven labelled boxes and ask them to write one shape per box as each clue is read; stretch: ask whether any other arrangement satisfies all five clues and justify the answer.

exercise.description: Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

items.prompt: Complete the weave grid below. The rule is: Row 1 — OVER 2, UNDER 1; Row 2 — UNDER 2, OVER 1; then repeat. Shade the OVER squares in the grid.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Strip 1 | Strip 2 | Strip 3 | Strip 4 | Strip 5 | Strip 6 |
| Row 1: OVER | OVER | UNDER | ... | ... | ... |
| Row 2: UNDER | UNDER | OVER | ... | ... | ... |
| Row 3: ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |
| Row 4: ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: OVER, OVER, UNDER, OVER, OVER, UNDER. Row 2: UNDER, UNDER, OVER, UNDER, UNDER, OVER. Row 3: same as Row 1. Row 4: same as Row 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the 2-over-1-under rule across each row, repeating the unit for the full width; repeat the 2-row unit for additional rows.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: complete Row 3 for the student and ask them to fill Row 4; stretch: ask the student to write the rule for a new mat where the unit is 3-over-2-under.

exercise.description: Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

items.prompt: On the grid on p.99, draw two different kites. Make sure the two kites are not identical — they should look different from each other. Label the two pairs of equal adjacent sides on each kite.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each kite must have two pairs of adjacent equal sides (not opposite). The two kites should differ in at least one dimension — one wider, one narrower, or oriented differently. Labels must correctly mark adjacent (not opposite) equal sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a diagonal axis line, then plot two pairs of adjacent equal sides on either side of the axis to form each kite.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show one completed kite with labelled sides and ask the student to draw a second with different proportions; stretch: ask the student to draw a kite that also happens to be a rhombus and explain why it qualifies as both.

exercise.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.

items.prompt: A solid cube is made from 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 small cubes. A tunnel is drilled straight through the cube from front to back along the central column, removing all small cubes in that column. How many small cubes are removed?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 small cubes are removed (the tunnel passes through 4 layers, removing 1 cube per layer in the central column).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of layers the tunnel passes through; each layer contributes one small cube to the removed column.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 4-row column on the side of the cube and ask the student to count the squares in that column; stretch: ask how many cubes would be removed if tunnels were drilled through the centre column in all three directions (accounting for the cube shared at the centre).

exercise.description: Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).

items.prompt: Rohan glues 27 small cubes into a 3 × 3 × 3 big cube and paints all faces of the big cube blue. How many small cubes have exactly 1 face painted blue?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 small cubes have exactly 1 face painted. These are the face-centre cubes — one at the centre of each of the 6 faces of the big cube. Each touches only one outer face.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify face-centre positions: one per face of the big cube, 6 faces total — each has exactly 1 painted face.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 3×3 grid for one face and ask the student to mark which square is in the centre; repeat for all 6 faces and count; stretch: ask the student to also find how many small cubes have exactly 2 faces painted and explain the position of those cubes.

exercise.description: Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.
